[P0040] This study successfully demonstrates the synthesis and characterization of BB, BC, BI, LPAC, and their corresponding BBAC, BCAC, and BIAC nanocomposites for solid-state supercapattery applications. The materials were prepared through distinct methods: co-precipitation for the bismuth oxyhalides, pyrolysis and chemical activation for LPAC, and ultrasonication for the composites. Structural and electrochemical analyses revealed BBAC as the standout material, possessing a superior specific surface area of 981 m2 g−1 compared to BCAC (783 m2 g−1) and BIAC (610 m2 g−1), which provides abundant active sites for electrolyte ion interaction. The enhanced electrochemical performance of the composites over their pristine constituents is attributed to their larger CV integrated areas, wider operational potential windows, and the synergistic interplay between the battery-type faradaic behavior of BiOX and the capacitive response of LPAC. Specifically, the BBAC electrode delivered a high current response of 93 mA at 10 mV s−1, facilitated by its nanosheet morphology and extensive surface area, coupled with a low charge transfer resistance (2.12 Ω) that ensures rapid ion transport. Leveraging these findings, practical solid-state supercapattery devices were constructed. The symmetric SSC (BBAC‖BBAC) device significantly outperformed its asymmetric ASC (BBAC‖LPAC) counterpart, achieving a high specific capacity of 476.46 C g−1 and an excellent power density of 6.5 kW kg−1, compared to 169.57 C g−1 and 5 kW kg−1 for the ASC. Both devices exhibited remarkable cycling stability, retaining 94.01% (ASC) and 98.10% (SSC) of their initial capacity after 2000 cycles. The collective metrics—outstanding specific capacity, broad voltage window (0–2.6 V), high energy density (172.06 Wh kg−1), superior power density (6.5 kW kg−1), and exceptional cyclability—firmly establish the BBAC nanocomposite as a highly efficient and promising electrode material for advanced symmetric solid-state supercapattery devices.

title: Clean energy storage devices in electricity market under dual carbon goals: assembly and performance of supercapacitors
config_paragraphs: [P0024] The electrochemical performance of the prepared electrode materials and assembled La-Ce-NiMoO₄//CNTs/SnO₂ asymmetric supercapacitors was systematically characterized by a series of electrochemical tests, including cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and long-term cycling stability tests. All tests were carried out in a three-electrode system (for single electrode) and two-electrode system (for asymmetric device) with a standard electrochemical workstation, using 6 mol·L⁻¹ KOH aqueous solution as the electrolyte. CV tests were performed to analyze the redox reaction characteristics and electrochemical reversibility of the materials under different voltage windows and scan rates; GCD tests were conducted to calculate the specific capacitance and energy density of the electrodes and devices under various current densities; EIS tests were carried out in the frequency range of 0.01 Hz to 100 kHz to evaluate the charge transfer resistance and ion diffusion resistance of the electrochemical system; long-term cycling stability tests were performed at a fixed current density to verify the structural stability and performance retention capability of the materials and devices after repeated charge-discharge cycles.
endpoint_paragraphs: [P0053] Figure 10 comprehensively characterizes the electrochemically relevant rate performance and cycle stability of La-Ce-NiMoO₄ through electrochemical CV curves at various scan rates, and GCD curves at various current densities, specific capacitance histogram plots, and rate cycle performance plots. Among them, in Fig. 10(a), the closed area of the CV curves at scan rates ranging from 5 to 80 mV s⁻¹ increases concomitantly with the elevation of scan rate, and the current response of the redox-related peaks continues to rise. Even at an elevated scan rate of 80 mV/s, the peak morphology does not show significant distortion30, with only a slight shift in peak position. This characteristic change proves that the material’s ionic diffusion and electronic transfer rates can quickly match the changes in potential scanning. Even at relatively high potential sweep rates, the electrode’s electrochemical reversibility the Faraday redox reaction can still be maintained, which is attributed to the high conductivity brought by La-Ce co-doping and the rapid mass transfer channels of the porous structure. In Fig. 10(b), under current densities of 1 to 10 A/g, the charge-discharge time of the GCD profiles gradually shortens with the increase in current, but the voltage platform remains clear. The symmetry of the curves is still good at high current densities, and the increase in IR drop is controllable. Combined with the histogram data in Fig. 10(c), a high specific capacitance of 2063 F/g is achieved by the material at 1 A/g, and upon increasing the current density to 10 A/g, the specific capacitance declines to 1148 F/g, still retaining 55.6% compared with the initial specific capacitance. This reflects that the material can still maintain a consistent pseudocapacitive energy storage mechanism under high-current charge-discharge conditions, with a high specific capacitance retention rate under high current density conditions, coupled with the retention of utilization efficiency for active sites is less affected by current density, showing excellent rate performance. The rate cycle curve in Fig. 10(d) shows that the specific capacitance remains stable with the number of cycles over a range of current densities, and when it is restored to 1 A/g, gravimetric specific capacitance can rise back to a level close to the initial value, verifying that the structure of the material is not prone to irreversible damage under variable current conditions, with excellent cycle durability. The above characterization results fully demonstrate the excellent electrochemical kinetic properties and structural stability of La-Ce-NiMoO₄. Overall, the material has a remarkably high specific capacitance, excellent rate capability and long-term cycling stability. These characteristics enable it to adapt to variable-rate working scenarios in the practical application of next-generation electrochemical energy storage devices such as supercapacitors, while ensuring the long-term service life of such energy storage devices.

[P0057] Figure 11(a) is a double logarithmic coordinate graph showing the good linear relationship between the redox peak current and the sweep rate (Iₚ) and the logarithm of the scan rate (logv) for the anode (black curve, slope b = 0.68) and the cathode (red curve, slope b = 0.62). In electrochemistry, the b-value is a crucial indicator for judging the kinetics of electrode reactions. When the b-value is approximately 0.5, the reaction is dominated by diffusion control; When the b-value ≈ 1.0, the reaction is governed by surface control. In this figure, b = 0.62 (cathode) and b = 0.68 (anode), indicating that the electrode reaction is co-dominated by controlled by both diffusion and surface-controlled processes, with the contribution of surface control being relatively more significant. This result can be utilized to reveal the intrinsic charge storage mechanism of materials and provide a basis for designing electrode materials with high rate performance. Figure 11(b) is a bar chart showing the capacitive contribution ratios of diffusion control (pink) and surface control (blue) to the total capacitance at various scan rates ranging from 5 to 100 mV s⁻¹. With an increase in the scan rate increases from 5 mV/s to 100 mV/s, the proportion of surface control decreases from 82% down to 61%, while the contribution of diffusion-controlled processes control increases from 18% down to 39%. At relatively low sweep rates, ions are afforded ample time to diffuse into the bulk of the electrode, resulting in a larger contribution from surface control. As the scan rate increases, the ion diffusion time is insufficient, the reaction mainly occurs on the electrode surface, and diffusion control becomes dominant. This figure clearly reflects the evolution of the kinetic process with the scan rate, which is helpful for optimizing the material structure (such as increasing mesopores/defects) to improve the capacitance retention rate at high rates. Figure 11(c) decomposes the cyclic voltammetry (CV) curve into the current contributions from surface control (cyan region, accounting for 39%) and diffusion control (yellow region), intuitively showing the current responses of the two processes at different potentials. Among them, the surface-controlled process (pseudocapacitance) usually has a faster charge transfer rate and better rate performance, while the diffusion-controlled process (battery-type behavior) provides higher capacity. Quantitatively separating the two contributions can accurately evaluate the charge storage mechanism of the electrode material, guiding the optimization of the ratio of surface-controlled to diffusion-controlled behavior through regulating material morphology, doping, or compounding, thereby obtaining electrode materials with high capacity and excellent rate capability. Figure 11(d) presents the cycling stability curve of La-Ce-NiMoO₄ at a current density of 3 A/g. The abscissa represents the number of cycles (0–5000 cycles), and the ordinate represents the capacitance retention rate (%). The initial specific capacitance of the material is 2063 F/g, and after 5000 charge-discharge cycles, the capacitance retention remains at 93%, with a corresponding specific capacitance of 1918 F/g. The overall curve shows a slow downward trend without obvious steep drops, with only slight capacitance decay occurring during the cycling process. This result intuitively reflects that La-Ce-NiMoO₄ has excellent cycle durability. The high capacitance retention after 5000 consecutive charge-discharge cycles proves that the crystal structure and porous morphology of the material did not undergo severe structural collapse or loss of active sites during repeated charge-discharge processes. The lattice stability and electronic structure optimization introduced by La-Ce co-doping effectively alleviated the problems of volume expansion and agglomeration of active components during charge-discharge. Meanwhile, the three-dimensional porous structure provides a continuous and stable channel for ion transport and charge transfer, reducing electrochemical polarization and energy loss during cycling. This excellent cycle stability provides key performance guarantee for the long-term practical application of La-Ce-NiMoO₄ in electrochemical energy storage devices for instance supercapacitors, and further verifies the effectiveness of the rare earth co-doping strategy in improving the cycle performance of transition metal molybdates. Figure (e) shows the SEM characterization image of La-Ce co-doped nickel molybdate material before cycling. The material exhibits a regular flower-like cluster structure assembled from a large number of two-dimensional flake-like nano-units. The edges of the flakes are flat, the thickness is uniform, and the flakes are stacked alternately to form a three-dimensional network with moderate porosity. The lateral size of a single flake is about several hundred nanometers to 1 μm. This complete and ordered structure provides unobstructed channels for electrolyte ion diffusion and electron conduction, and at the same time exposes sufficient electrochemical active sites, which is the structural basis for the material to have initial high specific capacity and good rate performance. Figure (f) is the SEM characterization image of the material after cycling. Compared with that before cycling, the edges of the flakes are obviously broken and curled, the regularity is significantly reduced, more slender needle-like/rod-like nanocrystals appear interspersed in the clusters, the overall morphology is more fluffy, the pore structure is more abundant but the order is reduced, and slight agglomeration occurs in some areas. On the one hand, this morphological evolution further increases the specific surface area of the material, exposes more active sites, reduces the ion diffusion resistance, and maintains or even improves the electrochemical activity to a certain extent. On the other hand, it also reflects that the material generates structural stress during repeated charge-discharge processes, with partial collapse and reconstruction. However, La-Ce doping effectively inhibits the complete pulverization of the material and delays the rapid loss of structural integrity through lattice pinning and defect passivation mechanisms. It not only buffers the volume strain during the cycling process but also retains the ion/electron transport channels as much as possible, enabling the material to achieve a balance among specific capacity, kinetic performance, and cycle life. Although the encapsulation of active sites and the increase in interface resistance after long-term cycling will gradually lead to capacity fading, the material still maintains a relatively efficient energy storage capacity overall.

[P0080] Guided by the increasing demand for high-performance efficiency and stability of clean energy storage apparatuses in the electricity market under the dual-carbon goals, this study designed and fabricated an asymmetric supercapacitor with La-Ce co-doped NiMoO₄ as the cathode and CNTs/SnO₂ composite as the anode. Through systematic structural characterization and electrochemical performance testing, the material modification mechanism and device energy storage characteristics were clarified: The hydrothermal method successfully achieved uniform co-doping of La and Ce elements in the NiMoO₄ lattice. XRD and XPS characterizations confirmed that the co-doping did not destroy the basic crystal structure of NiMoO₄, but significantly improved the material’s crystallinity, introduced abundant oxygen defects, and regulated the distribution of metal valence states. SEM, TEM, and nitrogen adsorption-desorption tests showed that La-Ce-NiMoO₄ exhibited a flower-like three-dimensional hierarchical porous structure with a specific surface area increased to 157.1 m²/g, providing ample active sites and efficient mass transfer pathways for electrochemical reactions. Electrochemical capability tests revealed that La-Ce co-doping synergistically optimized the electrochemical kinetic properties of NiMoO₄. The specific capacitance reached 2063 F/g at a specific current density of 1 A/g, which was significantly higher than that of the pure phase and single-doped samples. Moreover, it still maintained a capacity retention rate of 55.6% at a high current density of 10 A g⁻¹, as well as a 93% capacitance retention rate following 5000 cycles. Its excellent performance stems from the improved electron conduction efficiency, reduced ion diffusion resistance, and enhanced structural stability brought by co-doping. The CNTs/SnO₂ composite prepared with purified CNTs as the substrate, Through the close combination of SnO₂ nanoparticles and CNTs, the advantages of high capacity of SnO₂ are exerted, and the volume expansion problem of SnO₂ is alleviated by the three-dimensional conductive network of CNTs. The specific capacitive value reaches 312 F/g at 1 A/g, showing favorable rate performance and structural stability, rendering it an ideal anode material matching the La-Ce-NiMoO₄ cathode. In the field of aqueous zinc-ion batteries, Li and Han demonstrated that lithium nitrate (LiNO3) as a multifunctional additive can regulate Zn2+ solvation and promote controlled deposition, achieving over 500 stable cycles with an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.7% [5]. A comprehensive review by Zhao et al. systematically summarized four cathode energy storage mechanisms (Zn2+ insertion/extraction, H+/Zn2+ co-intercalation, chemical conversion, and dissolution/deposition) along with anode optimization strategies including artificial protective layers, electrolyte additives, and 3D porous structures [6]. endpoint_paragraphs: [P0001] Supercapacitors (SCs), as innovative energy storage devices, combine the rapid charge and discharge attributes of a capacitor with the energy storage characteristics inherent in batteries.1 SCs have been used in transportation, industry and electronic equipment.2,3 Electrochemical SCs can be categorized into electric double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) and pseudo-capacitors. In contrast to pseudo-capacitors, EDLCs exhibit superior cycle stability, heightened reversibility, and extended cycle life.4,5 Consequently, they have garnered increasing attention. The electrode material stands out as a pivotal component influencing the performance of SCs.6,7 Porous carbon materials emerge as ideal candidates for EDLCs owing to their attributes such as high specific surface area, excellent electrical conductivity, cost-effectiveness, and an optimized pore structure.8,9 Therefore, various carbon materials, such as activated carbon, carbon nanotubes, carbon aerogels (CAs), graphene and so on, have attracted wide attention in recent years.10,11 Biomass possesses a naturally organized, multi-scale hierarchical structure and incorporates heteroatoms such as nitrogen (N), oxygen (O), phosphorus (P), and other elements.12,13 The preparation of biomass-based carbon materials has the advantage of efficient treatment of biomass waste at the same time. Materials such as industrial cotton waste,14 bamboo,12 peanut shell,15 sisal leaf16 and lignin17 have been developed for high performance EDLC applications. Cellulose, the main component of plant biomass (more than 50%), is the most abundant and widely used biopolymer in nature;18 it can provide sustainable carbon precursors for energy storage. At present, Fischer, J. et al.19 have prepared a SC by using cellulose acetate as the precursor, and the specific surface area of the activated material could reach 1200 m2 g−1. In 4 M KOH, the active carbon electrode provides a specific capacitance of 186 F g−1 at a scanning speed of 10 mV s−1 and a high energy density of 40 W h kg−1 at a power density of 15 kW kg−1. N-doped porous carbon with large specific surface area (1973.3 m2 g−1) and large specific capacitance (120 F g−1 at 1.0 A g−1) was synthesized by direct pyrolysis of cellulose fibers in ammonia atmosphere. However, the porous carbon produced from biomass is greatly affected by impurities and the uncontrollability of pore structure limits its application.

[P0002] The ideal porous carbon for SC electrodes should contain layered pore structures of macropores, mesopores and micropores.20,21 Micropores can provide high capacitance; mesopores and macropores can provide ion transport channels and reduce diffusion resistance. CA is a kind of carbon material with three-dimensional layered porous structure, with macropores, mesopores and micropores, high specific surface area, good electrical conductivity and cyclic stability, so it is an ideal electrode material for supercapacitors.22 This layered structure enables ions to be diffused effectively through the carbon network. Using cellulose as carbon precursor, Zhou, H. et al.23 have prepared a graded porous CA as the carrier of conductive polymer polypyrrole (PPy). The hierarchical porous structure not only enables PPy to permeate and load evenly throughout the carbon network, but also ensures the rapid transfer of electrolytes and the high accessibility of PPy. The prepared hybrid material has high specific capacitance as high as 387.6 F g−1 (0.5 A g−1 in 1 M H2SO4) and excellent cycle stability (the capacity retention is 92.6% after 10 000 cycles). N-doped CAs prepared by Zhang, Z. et al.24 has high specific surface area, good wettability and electrical conductivity. When it is applied to SC, the specific capacitance reaches 253.7 F g−1 at a current density of 1 A g−1, and it still remains at 94.5% after 10 000 charge–discharge cycles. When the power density is 250 W kg−1, the energy density of the battery is 9.525 W h kg−1. NiS/N-doped carbon fiber aerogel nanocomposites were prepared by polymerization, carbonization and one-step solvothermal reaction.25 Using cotton fiber coated with dopamine as template, NiS nanoparticles were uniformly immobilized on the surface of NiS/N-doped carbon fiber aerogel. The layered nanocomposites showed excellent electrochemical performance of SCs with specific capacitance of 1612.5 F g−1, current density of 1 A g−1 and good cycle stability. However, the complex preparation process limits its large-scale production.

[P0035] In Fig. 7a, the excellent stability of CA-AA, CA-TB, CA-W, and CA-C is demonstrated after 5000 cycles of charge and discharge at a current intensity of 1 A g−1. The capacitance retention rates are remarkable, with values of 101.35%, 114.36%, 106.99%, and 99.07%, respectively. Notably, the capacitance of CA-AA, CA-TB, and CA-W exhibits an upward trend, showing a slight increase after 5000 cycles. This phenomenon may be attributed to the utilization of more micropores for ion storage over an extended cycle time, enhancing overall performance.39,40 In contrast, the specific capacitance of CA-C initially experiences a decline within the first 3000 cycles but gradually increases thereafter. This improvement in capacitance is attributed to the activation of the electrode's active sites, significantly enhancing the capacitance retention rate during the cycle.41,42 Subsequently, button-type SCs were assembled using CA-AA, CA-TB, CA-W, and CA-C, and they underwent testing under identical conditions in a two-electrode system (Fig. 7b). The capacitance retention rates for CA-AA, CA-TB, CA-W, and CA-C are impressive, reaching values of 102%, 131%, 104%, and 130%, respectively. The cyclic stability curves follow a similar trend to those observed in the three-electrode test. Notably, CA-C demonstrates a significant capacity increase, surpassing 130% after 5000 cycles, far exceeding the capacity retention rate observed in the three-electrode system. The enhanced cycle stability in the two-electrode system offers greater practical applicability for CA.43

[P0037] In electrochemical test, CA-AA prepared with acetic acid as anti-solvent has the best electrochemical performance and high specific capacitance (138 F g−1). When the power density is 181.06 W kg−1, it provides a high energy density of 10.06 W h kg−1. CA-AA also has excellent rate performance, and can still maintain a large specific capacitance (87%) at a current density of 10 A g−1. In addition, it has good cycle stability (the retention rate is 102% after 5000 cycles). The reason is that acetic acid is used as anti-solvent to adjust the hydrogen bonding strength, which makes the material form a developed pore structure and meets the requirements of supercapacitor electrodes with macropores, mesopores and micropores at the same time.

[P0117] Evaluating the long-term performance of supercapacitor electrodes is crucial. Therefore, we assessed the cyclic stability of our electrodes by monitoring their capacity retention (%) over 1000 consecutive charge-discharge cycles at a current density of 3 Ag-1. Fig. 10a and b depict the capacity retention results for both activated carbon (AC) and hybrid-composite (AC:MnO2) electrodes.

[P0121] For ideal supercapacitors, maintaining a high and stable capacitance over extended cycles is essential. Interestingly, all electrodes exhibited an initial stabilization phase, where capacitance remained relatively constant until approximately 200 cycles. However, beyond 200 cycles, a gradual decline in specific capacitance was observed for all samples. Notably, the decrease after 1000 cycles varied significantly across the AC electrodes: 4 % for AC-400 °C, 9.7 % for AC-500 °C, 23.6 % for AC-600 °C, and 40.8 % for AC-700 °C. This capacity loss is often attributed to the gradual decomposition of electroactive materials into the electrolyte during repeated charging and discharging. Over time, these cycles can lead to material breakdown and dissolution, ultimately reducing overall capacitance [ [41]].

[P0122] The hybrid-composite-electrodes (AC:MnO2-electrodes) presented a remarkably consistent trend in cyclic stability. In particular, the AC:MnO2-400 °C electrode showcased exceptional performance, retaining 99.4 % of its initial capacitance after 1000 cycles. This outstanding stability can be attributed to the presence of MnO2 in the composite. MnO2's intrinsic pseudocapacitive behavior and redox reactions likely play a crucial role in mitigating excessive material degradation during cycling, making it a promising candidate for applications demanding long cycle life [ [22,42]]. Interestingly, the AC-400°C-electrode without MnO2 addition, also demonstrated respectable cyclic stability, maintaining 97.1 % of its initial capacitance. This suggests that both carbonization temperature and material composition influence long-term performance.

[P0154] Optimal Performance at 400°C: The AC electrode prepared at 400 °C (AC-400 °C) emerged as the top performer, showcasing exceptional properties: a high surface area of 1432.4 m2g⁻1, specific capacitance of 183.4 Fg⁻1 in a 6 M KOH electrolyte and, impressive cyclic stability (94.3 % at 3 Ag⁻1).

[P0156] Hybrid composite Enhancement: Integrating MnO2 in a 1:1 ratio (AC:MnO2-400 °C) significantly boosted the AC's electrochemical performance. This hybrid composite electrode displayed a remarkable increase in specific capacitance (491.0 Fg⁻1), maintained exceptional cyclic stability (99.6 % at 3 Ag⁻1), and achieved a substantially higher energy density of 25.3 Whkg⁻1 at 187.3 Wkg⁻1 compared to its non-hybridized counterpart.

title: Rice Hull-Derived Carbon for Supercapacitors: Towards Sustainable Silicon-Carbon Supercapacitors
config_paragraphs: [P0006] Cyclic voltammetry (CV; at various scan rates and voltage ranges), galvanostatic charge/discharge tests (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS; from 0.01 Hz to 10 kHz with a potential amplitude of 50 mV) were performed on 0.01 g samples using an electrochemical workstation (IVIUM, Netherlands). The tests were conducted at room temperature using a three-electrode system, in which mercury/mercury oxide (Hg/HgO) was used as the reference electrode, a platinum sheet was used as the counter electrode, and 1 mol L−1 KOH solution served as the electrolyte. The working electrode was prepared by loading a slurry comprising 80 wt.% active material (e.g., biomass-based carbon composites that had been ball-milled for 24 h), 10 wt.% conducting agent (i.e., carbon black), and 10 wt.% binder (i.e., polytetrafluoroethylene in methanol) onto nickel foam. The obtained samples were mixed with carbon black and polytetrafluoroethylene in a ratio of 8:1:1, and the appropriate amount of pyrrolidone solution was added to the mixture. In order to mix the sample uniformly, it was sonicated for 15 min. A small amount of the mixed liquid was sucked up by the syringe, and the liquid was evenly dropped on the nickel sheet. The nickel sheet needed to be dried at 105 °C for 12 h, which was extruded by a sheeter under a pressure of 6 MPa for 30 s. The specific capacitance and energy density were measured after three repeated GCD experiments to obtain the average value.

[P0016] The electrochemical performances of the as-prepared carbon materials were measured by CV and GCD tests in a three-electrode system with 1 M KOH aqueous electrolyte (Figure 7). The cyclic voltammograms of the samples under various conditions obtained at a scan rate of 50 mV s−1 are displayed in Figure 7a. The voltammograms adopted a nearly rectangular shape without clear oxidation or reduction peaks, which indicated that the capacitance of the electrode was supplied almost entirely by the electrostatic double-layer conductor (EDLC) [47,48]. Additionally, the integrated area of the closed CV curve reflects the capacitance of electrode materials. The CVs of RH-900 and Act-RH-900 had the largest areas at the scan rate of 50 mV s−1, indicating that they obtained the maximum capacitance values. These results were attributed to their micro/mesoporous structures, reasonable pore distributions, and content of disordered graphitization structures [49]. To further explore the reason for the superior capacitor performance of RH-900 and Act-RH-900, the CV curves were obtained at various scan rates (10–100 mV s−1), and the results are shown in Figure 7c,e, respectively. The curve shapes remained generally stable as the scan rates increased, which confirmed the stable carbon structure of the samples [50]. Meanwhile, the integrated areas of the CV closed curves increased with the increasing scan rate, regardless of the voltage window. The most noticeable effect on the CV areas corresponded to a voltage window of –1 to 0 V for RH-900, and –1 to 0.4 V for Act-RH-900, which indicated that supercapacitor electrodes comprising RH-900 and Act-RH-900 could accommodate significant energy storage [51]. Longer discharge times were observed for RH-900 and Act-RH-900 (Figure 7b), thus demonstrating the superior capacitance properties of these two materials. As shown in Figure 7d,f, RH-900 and Act-RH-900 exhibited quasi-isosceles triangle shapes when the electrodes were charged to 0.3 V, and the longer discharge times corresponded to a current density of 0.5 A g−1.

[P0019] The symmetric SCs were further explored depending on the better capacitive performance of Act-RH-900 in the three-electrode system. The symmetric SCs (Act-RH-900//Act-RH-900) were tested in the two-electrode system in 1 M KOH aqueous electrolyte. Figure 9a shows the CV graph of Act-RH-900//Act-RH-900 working in the scan range of 10–100 mV s−1. The voltammograms adopted a nearly rectangular shape without clear oxidation or reduction peaks, which indicated that the capacitance of the electrode was supplied almost entirely by the electrostatic double-layer conductor (EDLC). The curve shapes remained generally stable as the scan rates increased, which confirmed that Act-RH-900//Act-RH-900 could withstand a wide voltage from 0 to 1 V, and also proved the stable structure of the sample carbon material. The highly symmetrical triangle shape for the GCD curves of Act-RH-900//Act-RH-900 at different current densities of 0.3, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, and 10 A g−1 is displayed in Figure 9b, which indicates that the sample shows ideal capacitive behavior because of the structure of the material. According to Equations (1) and (2), a single-electrode specific capacitance of 89.28 F g−1 at a current density of 0.3 A g−1 for Act-RH-900//Act-RH-900 has been calculated by discharging time. Act-RH-900//Act-RH-900 has obtained an excellent energy density of 12.4 Wh kg−1 and power density of 175 W kg−1 in the 1 M KOH electrolyte calculated by the Equations (3) and (4). A representative Nyquist plot (from EIS measurements) for the Act-RH-900//Act-RH-900 is displayed in Figure 9c and the Bode phase angle plot is presented in Figure 9d. The phase angle of Act-RH-900//Act-RH-900 in the low-frequency region was about –79°. The angle was between –90° (ideal capacitor) and –45° (pseudo-capacitor), which indicated intercalation capacitance in the Act-RH-900//Act-RH-900 materials. These results are similar to the three-electrode test results. The Ragone plot of Act-RH-900//Act-RH-900 is shown in Figure 9e. The power density decreased as the energy density increased.
endpoint_paragraphs: [P0018] Representative Nyquist plots (from EIS measurements) for the samples are displayed in Figure 8a. The phase angle reached 45° in the low-frequency region, revealing the attendance of supercapacitor performance. In the high-frequency region, the Act-RH-900 curve exhibited a smaller slope, which indicated lower impedance. The extension line value crossing the horizontal axis represents the solution resistance (Rs), and the Rs of Act-RH-900 is smaller than the other samples, which shows that the working electrode made by Act-RH-900 suffers relatively low resistance in the energy-storage process. This is due to the fact that the unique pore structure can be adequately accessed by ions to reduce the resistance of the electrode material, and the silicon-containing functional groups can improve the conductivity of the materials. These results further highlighted the advantage of Act-RH-900 for application as an electrochemical energy-storage material [58]. The Bode phase angle plots of RH-900 and Act-RH-900 are presented in Figure 8b. The phase angles of RH-900 and Act-RH-900 in the low-frequency region were about –77° and –84°, respectively. These angles were between –90° (ideal capacitor) and –45° (pseudo-capacitor), which indicated intercalation capacitance in the RH-900 and Act-RH-900 materials [59]. The RH-900 and Act-RH-900 feature frequency corresponding to a phase angle of –45° is 0.23 and 0.38 Hz, respectively. The time constant of RH-900 and Act-RH-900 can reach to 4.35 and 2.63 s, respectively, which are much smaller than 10 s (the time constant of conventional activated carbon SCs). The smaller time constant demonstrated that there was a faster charge/discharge rate, and the rate of Act-RH-900 is smaller than that of RH-900. Meanwhile, RH-900 and Act-RH-900 achieved capacitance retentions greater than 81.56% and 87.88%, respectively, after 5000 cycles (Figure 8c). These results illustrate the excellent cycling stability and electrochemical reversibility of the Act-RH-900 sample in particular [60]. The pore size distribution and defect structure of the Act-RH-900 sample have important effects on the material’s electrochemical energy-storage properties: the micropores provide storage space, and mesopores provide channels for ion transport, while the defect structure enhances the ion contact area [61,62]. The synergism among the micro- and meso-porous structural characteristics enables efficient electrochemical transport and storage.
